title: How Videos Helped Me Uncover Abuse at an Arkansas Private School
content:
The Delta Institute for the Developing Brain was set back off a country road in a white colonial house — such an atypical location that I first drove right by it, unsure that it was a school. I turned around, went to the door, introduced myself as a reporter and asked for a tour.

I knew a student had been assaulted in this Arkansas school a year earlier because of some news reports based on a detective’s description. Once inside, I noted the preteens tucked into hammock chairs or sitting on the floor. I noted the cameras mounted in the foyer and classrooms, a reminder that, in order to fully understand what had happened, I’d need to see the video that had captured the assault. 

But since this happened at the Delta Institute, a private school, I didn’t have access to the types of public records — incident reports, emails and video — that might have existed at a public school. The only reason we knew that something awful had happened here was that law enforcement got involved. I would have to keep reporting for weeks until the criminal case was closed. Then I could start pursuing the video evidence.

title: Access to finance ‘strengthens climate resilience’ among sub-Saharan women
content:
Empowering women through greater access to finance could “strengthen” households’ resilience to “climate shocks”, according to a new study.  

Published in Climate Risk Management, it analyses the impact of financial access on “women-headed households” in sub-Saharan Africa. 

The study finds that where women had formal financial access – such as through owning a bank account – households were more able to withstand short-term shocks.

It adds that “climate shocks”, such as extreme weather events and the impacts of climate change, can cause economic crises, which destabilise communities and households. 

However, the authors say that in order to protect households from long-term climate vulnerabilities – including “droughts, floods and sea-level rise” – financial access would need to be paired with wider efforts to tackle gender inequality. 

They add that the findings could have important implications for policy in sub-Saharan Africa, where many countries and households are vulnerable to climate disasters. 

The study highlights that entrenched gender disparities mean many women still have unequal access to financial services in sub-Saharan Africa

title: Beyond mandates: making data sharing count
content:
"That is substantial progress. But a requirement to deposit data is not the same as an incentive to make data genuinely reusable. A file can be technically available yet impossible to interpret; a repository record can lack documentation, provenance or a workable licence; and a data-availability statement can say “available on request” even when requests are rarely answered. Compliance can establish a floor. It cannot, by itself, create a culture in which careful stewardship is rewarded.

The policy story can be read in three stages. The first made sharing permissible and encouraged it. The second made planning, deposition and access conditions more explicit. We are now entering a third stage: recognition. The central question is no longer only whether data were shared, but whether the sharing was useful—and whether the people who did the difficult work receive credit."

title: Lab Owner Suspected of $547 Million Medicare Fraud Extradited to The United States
content:
A laboratory owner who spent more than three years as a fugitive has been returned to the United States to face charges over what prosecutors describe as a nationwide scheme to bill Medicare $547 million for medically unnecessary cancer tests.

Khalid Ahmed Satary, 54, was arrested on July 20 by unnamed “regional partners” in the Middle East while carrying a fake Mexican passport under a false name, the U.S. Department of Justice said this week. He appeared in federal court in Virginia and faces health care and wire fraud, kickback, and money laundering conspiracy charges. He has not been convicted, and the most serious counts carry up to 20 years in prison.

Between 2016 and 2019, prosecutors say, Satary controlled Clio Laboratories in Georgia, Performance Laboratories in Oklahoma, and Lazarus Services in Louisiana. Patient recruiters and telemarketing call centers targeted Medicare beneficiaries by phone and at health fairs, while telemedicine doctors allegedly approved cancer genetic tests without treating and often without even speaking to the patients.

title: State of the climate: Rapidly developing El Niño raises chance of record-warm 2026
content:
As 2026 passes its halfway point, the world is watching one of the most rapidly intensifying El Niño events in the modern record take shape in the tropical Pacific.

The developing El Niño is boosting expectations for global temperatures, both this year and next.

El Niño is the warm phase of a recurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere, temporarily raising global temperatures and reshaping rainfall and extreme weather around the world.

Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” report in April gave 2026 a 19% chance of setting a new global temperature record. 

That chance now stands at 35% – a near-doubling in four months – with virtually all of the change driven by ever-stronger El Niño forecasts.

The key findings from the first half of 2026 include:

  • The first six months of 2026 were the third-warmest start to a year on record – around 1.4C above pre-industrial levels – behind only 2024 and 2025. 
  • While the first few months of the year came in as the fourth or fifth warmest, both May and June were the second-warmest ever recorded as El Niño conditions took hold.
snippet: As 2026 passes its halfway point, the world is watching one of the most rapidly intensifying El Niño events in the modern record take shape in the tropical Pacific.

title: EU Targets Georgian Oil Refinery Over Russian Crude Processing
content:
The European Union included a Georgian oil refinery that processes Russian crude into its new sweeping sanctions package aimed at crippling Moscow’s war economy.

The Council of the European Union adopted the restrictive measures—the 21st package—on Thursday, establishing a mechanism to prohibit transactions with refineries in third countries that help generate revenue for Russia. Under this framework, the EU is imposing a transaction ban on the Kulevi refinery that will enter into force in six months.

RFE/RL, citing a source in Brussels, reported that the EU's Official Journal lists January 25, 2027, as the date the ban takes effect. A separate source told the outlet that the six-month deferred mechanism is the first of its kind in the EU's sanctions practice.

“With each round of sanctions, we squeeze Russia’s economy and its capacity to prolong its illegal war,” Kaja Kallas, the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, said in the Council’s statement.

title: Facilitating green open access through faculty–library collaboration: A case study from the University of Hong Kong - ScienceDirect
content: Abstract: This article presents a case study of a green open access initiative undertaken by the University of Hong Kong Libraries in collaboration with the Faculty of Engineering. The project aimed to increase the availability of journal articles in HKU Scholars Hub, the institutional repository, by collecting and depositing accepted manuscripts. Publication records from 2020 to 2024 were identified and matched with external open access versions using the Unpaywall API. Publisher self-archiving policies and embargo periods were identified using the Sherpa API. Current Faculty members were then invited to submit accepted manuscripts for eligible publications. title: UK Freezes $30 million in London Properties Owned by a Man Under Investigation in Singapore Money Laundering Case
content:
Britain’s National Crime Agency has frozen at least $33 million of properties owned by Xu Haika, a Chinese, Cambodian and Vanuatu national who has been identified as a suspect in a $2.3 billion Singapore money laundering case previously covered by OCCRP.

Land registry records obtained by Transparency International UK and shared with OCCRP show that the National Crime Agency lodged freeze orders for Xu Haika’s properties on June 5 this year.

OCCRP first reported on Xu Haika’s portfolio of U.K. real estate in November 2025, which include 16 luxury apartments in two adjoining new build developments, in the heart of central London’s Tottenham Court Road.

Xu Haika did not reply to questions sent to Flanton & Co, the accountancy firm that registered his two U.K. companies that own the properties. Neither he nor Flanton & Co responded to previous questions about his properties or his links to the Singapore criminal case.

While Xu Haika has not been criminally charged in the U.K., the NCA freezing order was granted under civil recovery legislation which allows law enforcement to target property suspected of being derived from unlawful conduct.

title: European Commission publishes call for evidence on AI strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors
content:
The European Commission’s strategy will set out a vision to support the Cultural and Creative Sectors (CCS) while fostering innovation and safeguarding European cultural and linguistic diversity.

The opportunities and challenges presented by AI in the CCS are complex, spanning technical, economic and societal dimensions. This call for evidence aims to gather information and stakeholders’ views to help develop a strategy that will ensure AI complements, rather than replaces, human creativity; supports broader access to culture and knowledge; and contributes to a fair, sustainable, innovative and competitive European creative economy.

The consultation is open to anyone, including artists, creators, rights holders, professional associations, AI providers, developers, researchers and public authorities with cultural and AI policy expertise, as well as members of the public with an interest in the future of culture and creativity in the age of AI.

Help shape the future AI strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors with your views until 11 September 2026.

Link to the public consultation website of the European Commission.

title: Taistelutahto vaatii runojen ylevyyttä ja ilakoivaa huumoria
content:
Se uljainkin upseeri joutuu vuorollaan tappiomielialan valtaan, ja silloin pitää kavereiden vieressä tsempata. Koska harvoin sisäinen epäröinti näkyy ulospäin, varmuuden vuoksi kaikissa maailman armeijoissa on kehitetty yleviä seremonioita ja marssilauluja puhaltamaan meihin voimaa.

Kun talvisodan henkeä pidettiin yllä, ylevyydellä oli siinä oma roolinsa. Se kuitenkin nyppi osaa sotilaista, sillä heistä tuntui ymmärrettävästi siltä, että kotirintamalla puhutaan suuta suuremmalla. Suurempi painoarvo oli Yrjö Jylhän runoilla. Hänet tunnettiin urhoollisena upseerina ja tiedettiin hänen kirjoittavan maailmasta, jonka todellakin tuntee. Siksi hän oli niin tärkeä.

Todennäköisesti kuitenkin tärkein taistelutahdon ylläpitäjä oli näyttelijä Aku Korhosen esittämä valheentorjuntapäällikkö radiossa. Ylipäänsä riemukkailla urheilukisoilla, huumorilla ja viihdeohjelmilla oli ja on korvaamaton merkitys mielialoille.

title: The Tombstone Edition that Helped Galvanize American Independence
content:
It’s known as the Tombstone Edition, a lightning-strike newspaper image that presages the American Revolution — and 261 years after it electrified readers in Colonial-era Philadelphia, a rare, fragile copy now rests at the Library.

Pennsylvania Journal editor and printer William Bradford, livid at Britain’s imposition of the Stamp Act on the Colonies, laid out the front page of his Oct. 31, 1765, newspaper as if it were the paper’s grave marker, complete with a skull and crossbones set at the top in heavy black type. His furious editorial said the Stamp Act’s tax on paper, a rare and expensive commodity, would kill his newspaper, others like it and therefore choke off a free press.

“EXPIRING,” read the headline, describing the paper’s fate.

“The Liberty of the Press has been very justly one of the main Pillars of the Liberty of the People,” read the front-page editorial, blasting the act as “insupportable Slavery.”

title: Advocating for Digital Accessibility: An Interview with Junior Fellow Mia Giancola
content:
In this interview, 2026 Library of Congress Junior Fellow Mia Giancola discusses working on the Year of Digital Accessibility in the Library’s IT Design & Development Directorate. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Pedro: It’s great to have you on our team this summer. Could you tell us what you are working on?

Mia: Hi! I’m so excited to be here! I’d love to: I am a Junior Fellow working on the Digital Accessibility Team in the Design Division. The Digital Accessibility Team runs an accessibility educational initiative every year called the “Year of.” This year is the “Year of Magnification.” A great way to think of magnification is pinch and zoom, which many people use daily. Magnification is important when considering low vision or blind users, older adults, smartphone users, and several other key populations. In addition to informational materials, I have created an interactive game to help demonstrate the ways magnification can impact how people access digital content, including library resources and collections.

P: Tell us a bit about your background and journey. What professional or educational experiences led you to apply for this fellowship?

title: Body is a Lost Media, Pixels Are All You’re Gonna See – Reframing the Blur and the Body Across Palestine Online
content:
I remember scrolling the Instagram account @eyeonpalestine for months, and how you start to feel like when you stay there long enough and become doomed by a sensation, becoming a fog. The feeling is both physical and emotional. It’s like being somewhere after an explosion. You got blurry vision, your ears are buzzing.

Some images are clear, unfiltered, and painful as they were meant to be: bodies, rubble, blood. Others are covered. Blurred. There is apparently no legible criteria, no consistent logic you can extract from what gets blurred and what does not. Extremely violent images sometimes appear in full while others, less graphic, less explicit, are swallowed by a grey screen, a pixelated veil, and a sign that resembles a blinded eye, an eye with an arrow upon it. The signs of what Instagram calls “sensitive content warning.”

From Exactly That Body: Images Against Oppression, Kateryna Iakovlenko, e-flux Journal, Issue #133

title: Wikimedia Sverige och Wikimedia Brasil får Sida-finansiering för att stärka civilsamhället kring fri kunskap
content:
Wikimedia Sverige och den brasilianska systerorganisationen Wikimedia Brasil har beviljats finansiering från Sida för ett gemensamt ettårigt projekt som ska stärka det civila samhällets möjligheter att skapa och sprida tillförlitlig, fri kunskap i Brasilien.

Projektet, Strengthening Civil Society Capacity for Open Knowledge through Wikimedia Brasil, pågår från oktober 2026 till september 2027. I fokus står två så kallade community-hubbar i delstater där digital kunskapsproduktion idag är underrepresenterad. Genom lokala partnerskap med volontärer, kulturinstitutioner, universitet och civilsamhällesorganisationer ska projektet bidra till att dokumentera kulturarv, geografisk information och lokal kunskap – och göra den fritt tillgänglig via Wikipedia, Wikimedia Commons och Wikidata.

Projektet knyter också an till flera verktyg inom Wikimediarörelsen, bland annat Metabase (en databas för kompetens och kunskapsdelning) och Capacity Exchange (en global plattform för mentorskap). Det knyter även an till Wikispeech, där Wikimedia Brasilien driver en pilotinsats för att samla in talinspelningar på underrepresenterade språk, i samarbete med Wikimedia Sverige.

title: EU’s Google fine risks triggering Trump as he gears up for more tariffs
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Union knew its €890 million fine against Google risked poking the bear in Washington. And the timing couldn’t be worse.

President Donald Trump, who’s lashed out at previous EU fines against U.S. tech companies, is in the final hours of deciding a new regime of tariffs, expected when a temporary 10 percent levy is due to expire Friday. That hastily imposed global tax on imports was imposed after the U.S. Supreme Court had struck down Trump’s “Liberation Day”  global tariffs in February. 

The fear in Europe is that Thursday’s fine — the highest-ever imposed for violation of the EU’s signature Digital Markets Act that regulates major tech platforms — could trigger Trump to respond in what he sees as a tit-for-tat trade war.

title: Beyond the Ballot Box: Democracy Is What Happens Between Elections
content:
Democracy, for me, means accountable institutions anchored in the rule of law. It is not just about elections. Rather, it is everything that happens between elections to ensure people have access to three core values: dignity, safety, and a sense of belonging to a healthy and free society.

Moldova is experiencing the ruptures in the international rules-based order deeply. As Ukraine’s neighbour, we are close to the frontline of its efforts to defend its sovereignty and European security. From the first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion, we have faced threats to our own security, concerted efforts to undermine our democratic institutions, and a huge influx of refugees.[1]

Moldova is a small country of 2.6 million people, yet in the first months of the war we hosted nearly one million Ukrainian refugees. Our society has not fractured – and Moldovan civil society has been instrumental in sustaining that cohesion, working alongside government and international partners.

title: Who decides if and how AI is used? Self-determination should be the priority, say Mayan activists from Chiapas
content:
Maya activists reflect on AI, autonomy, and decision-making as part of a hybrid workshop

Originally published on Rising Voices

Opinion spectrometer activity at the in-person workshop that took place in San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas on May 5, 2026. Photo by Yulma Rodríguez and used with permission.

Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and peer-learning are important tools to highlight and strengthen Indigenous self-determination and to support Indigenous communities in informed decision-making regarding the use and application of AI in their contexts. This was the focus of the hybrid workshop, “Artificial intelligence, accountability, and Indigenous self-determination,” organized by Rising Voices (Global Voices) during the months of April and May 2026.

On May 5-7, 2026, within the framework of the Mayan Languages Digital Activism Summit in San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas, fifteen Mayan languages digital activists took part in the in-person activity to collectively discuss IA, autonomy, and informed decision making by Indigenous communities.
